knowledge_abstraction.bug_theme: Complex unary numerical precision degradation at extreme magnitudes
knowledge_abstraction.general_principle: Complex floating-point kernels may use magnitude-dependent algorithms that lose precision or overflow/underflow for extreme real or imaginary components, causing deviation from reference implementations.

risk_dimensions.dtype: complex64 and complex128 with large-magnitude real or imaginary components

failure_mechanism.description: Complex unary operators may evaluate intermediate quantities that are sensitive to extreme magnitudes, leading to precision loss, overflow, or underflow in the computed real or imaginary parts.

input_exploration: Vary complex real and imaginary components across logarithmic or exponential magnitude scales
Include negative, positive, mixed-sign, and pure imaginary complex values
Test both complex64 and complex128 precision levels
constraint_awareness: CPU complex numerical kernels may diverge from NumPy or higher-precision references
Tolerances must account for complex dtype precision limits and magnitude-dependent error
Extreme component magnitudes can trigger intermediate overflow or underflow
oracle_strategy: Compare outputs against NumPy or a higher-precision reference for the same complex inputs
Flag numerical mismatches outside magnitude-aware tolerances
Monitor for NaN, Inf, or unexpected finite deviations from the reference

transferability.reason: The underlying risk affects complex numerical operators beyond torch.sqrt, including elementwise functions such as exp, log, trigonometric, and other arithmetic kernels that rely on magnitude-dependent complex arithmetic.

important_considerations: Target complex unary and related elementwise numerical operators on CPU and possibly other backends
Explore extreme magnitude regions rather than fixed reproduction values
Use precision-aware oracles that account for complex64 versus complex128 behavior
generation_strategy: Generate complex tensors using magnitude sweeps and varied sign/phase patterns, then compare outputs to NumPy or higher-precision references with appropriate tolerances. Focus on numerical consistency across complex dtypes and avoid hard-coded historical trigger values.
